$comment: Authoritative attestation reference for the production publicai-gateway CVM. Fetched at runtime by the /proof page. composeHash was read back from the CVM's RTMR3 event log on 2026-08-31 and cross-checked against the Phala control-plane API; both report 3392da4d. Image digests are the linux/amd64 children of the cosign-signed proof-v23 index for sub2api (INDEX 48e96b81) built by publish-tee-images run 33377359684 from commit b6f903328; the attestor image is deliberately left at its proof-v20 pin (INDEX cef1d03d) because deploy/attestor was not touched, and repinning it would widen the attested surface for nothing. VERIFICATION SCOPE, stated plainly: composeHash, osImageHash, the image digests and the build commit were each read back from a live source, and composeHash was cross-checked against two independent ones. The cosign keyless signature was NOT verified locally for this release - the workflow performs the signing and its run succeeded, and anyone can verify certificate identity https://github.com/FiiLabs/sub2api/.github/workflows/publish-tee-images.yml@refs/heads/feat/two-sided-market plus the embedded githubWorkflowSha against the sourceCommit below, but this file does not claim it was done. This release fixes two independent defects in operational alerting, found after a P0 alert email fired for a non-incident. The trigger: in a one-minute window carrying three requests, one client aborted its upload mid-body, producing a 400 owned by the client that never reached an upstream account - one in three is 33.33 percent, over the 20 percent threshold. The day before, twelve alerts of the same kind fired with readings of 100, 80 and 61.5 percent, none of which were outages; they were minutes containing one or two requests. Those alerts had never been delivered because the alert recipient list was empty, so configuring a recipient is what exposed them. First fix: rate-based alert rules now require a minimum sample size. The previous guard admitted any window containing at least one request, which at low traffic is a noise generator. The threshold of twenty follows from a stated principle - a single failure must never be able to trip an alert - since one failure in twenty is exactly five percent and the most sensitive rule is strictly greater than five. Second fix: the SLA error definition counted client-owned errors against the platform. It filtered on status code alone, while the three adjacent upstream-error counters all discriminate on error_owner. This is not a new policy but the completion of an existing one: the definition already excluded business-limited errors on the grounds that a rule working as intended is not a fault, and client-owned errors are the same category. The expression is now a single shared constant because it has two call sites, the overview and the trend chart, whose divergence would be invisible - each correct on its own while disagreeing with the other. Note that this shifts historical dashboard figures: error rate falls and SLA rises, because excluded requests leave both the numerator and the denominator. Error totals are unchanged and still count every owner. Alert rule 8 was separately reconfigured from a one-minute to a five-minute window, matching the other seven rules. Earlier in this line: proof-v22 (attach-time probe, abuse alerts made visible), v21 (supplier self-service re-authorization), v20 (supply concurrency 3->15), v19 (abuse detection, shipped disabled), v18, v17, v16/v15. osImageHash, appId and instanceId are unchanged; the deploy passed --no-dev-os explicitly, because phala deploy silently switches to a dev OS image when it detects a local SSH key and a dev OS would void the attestation. This rollout completed in 86 seconds with no incident.
